subject: Range Residency and Variogram Pattern Interpretations

messages.author: 2e9fefa3b01ef3a2
messages.subject: Range Residency and Variogram Pattern Interpretations
parts:
Hello Everyone,

I am estimating home range (HR) size for a population of hawks. I’m new to this type of analysis, and despite exploring the excellent resources from Chris and this group, I'm still seeking confirmation regarding range resident (RR) individuals. I apologize for revisiting this topic repeatedly and for the redundancy in some of the variograms I’m showing. Perhaps it could serve as a fun challenge for someone, or at least continue to shed light on certain patterns not only for myself but also for others.

I've categorized 21 birds into different groups:

1-7: Those I think most likely be RR but could use another pair of eyes on

8-21: More confusing patterns. I think might need segmentation but could use advice on how to move forward

22&23: Individuals I don’t think are RR

As variogram interpretation is essential for using this methodology, I would greatly appreciate any help validating/refuting RR in these birds and advice on how to move forward for the more complicated birds (8-21). I've included some notes based on observation of behaviors, raw trajectories, and basic segmentation (segclust2d).


A few additional notes:

  • These are fully zoomed out variograms - I'm not confident on the extent of the variogram to consider when determining RR and how much to “disregard” as I’ve read several times the last half of the variogram isn’t that useful and the general variogram function in CTMM package displays ~50% for this reason. I suspect many of the birds I'm unsure about might also exhibit RR characteristics if only considering this extent
  • Birds are tracked for different amounts of time (start dates vary from June 2022-March 2023). We switched from a 20-minute fix rate to a 1-hour fix rate late 2023. About 75% of the variograms contain this interval change in their final month.
  • Some birds display multiple disjunct space use areas, and they commute to these areas on a daily or weekly basis. A few birds have engaged in longer forays, remaining away for several days or weeks before returning to stationary areas.
  • I do have an error model incorporated in my data, CI= Gauss doesn’t work on my computer for this large dataset, but the confidence intervals look ok as is to me
  • All fits (not shown here) diverged on either OU or OUF models (even birds 22&23) 
Thank you - I appreciate you and your time

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Range Residency and Variogram Pattern Interpretations
parts:
Hi Amy,

1-7 look pretty good, but you do want to confirm that the fitted model matches the general features of the empirical variogram.
Is there a big gap in the data causing 8-10 to look like that?
11-16 are messy, but not terrible.
17-23 may require the segmented estimates. This will be more obvious when contrasting against theoretical variogram of the fitted model.
With 23, you could segment spatially and then mean() the two estimates together.

Best,
Chris

messages.author: 2e9fefa3b01ef3a2
messages.subject: Re: Range Residency and Variogram Pattern Interpretations
parts:
Hi Chris, 

Thank you for the fast reply and for lending a trained eye.

I've reattached the variograms with fitted models for reference. I've been running these as ctmm.select in parallel within a foreach loop and I have noticed some models converge better when limiting the number of iterations (~70) and others when no limit is put on the iteration. Do you have any idea why?  Those with strong RR (not shown here) converge consistently no matter the limit, but these with more tricky movements tend to vary. 

After comparing the model fits, 
For 1-10 - Do you think we can consider them as RR? Birds 8-10 only have a few (2-4) half days worth of fixes skipped throughout the entire duration of their tracking periods 
For 11-16 - Do you think we can consider them as RR? 
For 17-23 - Do all need more work? 
For 23  (and other individuals commuting between multiple areas) - Is it generally more biologically sound to calculate the average of multiple HR areas or to simply add them together, and possibly exclude the commuting pathways?

all the best,
Amy

What do you mean by the number of iterations?

Most of these are okay to good, but 22-23 are poor - from both the overall trend and the big white area between the theoretical and empirical estimates, where their CIs don't overlap.

I would include the area between as well, if it makes sense to segment a third commuting state.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Range Residency and Variogram Pattern Interpretations
parts:
Hello Chris,

Thank you, it's greatly appreciated.

Regarding iterations, I was referring to adjusting the "maxit" argument inside the control parameter within the ctmm.select function. Running all my individuals was at one time was very time-consuming (~a week) so I started exploring different optimization methods. I observed that by limiting the iterations (e.g., maxit=70), certain models exhibited slightly better convergence (see example). However, I was just inquiring with you out of curiosity and haven't yet compared the overall akde outcomes. 

Best,

Amy

messages.subject: AKDE error meta analysis
parts:
Hi Chris,

I have another question I hope you can help with.  I’m  working through the meta- analysis with the hopes of running a PKDE for my population. When I run akde() on my telemetry data set and fits list, I run into the following error: “Error in if (isotropic) { : the condition has length > 1”

I was successful at running this on an earlier subset, but I have some individuals in my population that commuted or shifted their ranges between multiple areas. I segmented these individuals based on behavioral states and used mean() to combine. Now the akde isn’t liking the data I’m feeding into it. Perhaps this was the wrong approach. Could this be throwing things off?

Best,

amy

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: AKDE error meta analysis
parts:
Hi Amy,

Sorry for the delay. If you segmented based on behavior and estimated behavior-specific movement models, then I would also calculate AKDEs for each behavior and then run mean() on the AKDEs with sample=FALSE.
Otherwise, you would be calculating a one-behavior AKDE with the average-behavior autocorrelation model.

Best,
Chris
